titulo.texto: Wooden Mask and Crown of the Dance of the Negritos

frase_gancho.texto: A smiling black mask that recalls those who arrived from across the sea.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the dance mask we move on to the festive hairstyle of Huastec women. Look for a headdress made of skeins of colored yarn that circles the head like a crown.

guion_corto.texto: This carved wooden mask, painted a glossy black and with smiling features, is used in the Danza de los Negritos, which is danced among the Totonac and Nahua Peoples of Veracruz and the highlands of Puebla. It has pronounced eyebrows, a mustache, and open eyes to see through. The dancer also wears a straw hat lined with fabric and covered with colored ribbons. The dance is a kind of theater: a story told through dance, with violin and footwork, in which, according to tradition, an African worker is bitten by a snake and healed with songs and music. It is a reminder that the Gulf had a population of African origin from the colonial period onward.

guion_largo.texto:
This mask smiles, and it has good reason to: the Danza de los Negritos is a celebration. But behind the smile lies a story centuries long, one that tells how the peoples we now call Mexico met and mingled. And it is a good way to close a hall that has spoken of the Huastec, the Totonac, and the Nahua Peoples.

Let us begin with the context. The port of Veracruz was the main point of entry for enslaved Africans into New Spain. Many worked on the sugar mills, the cattle ranches, and the ports of the Gulf. Some escaped and formed free communities. One of the most famous was that of Yanga, an African leader who founded, in the early seventeenth century, a town that is considered one of the first free towns of Africans in the Americas. Today it bears his name.

With that history in mind, you understand the dance better. The dancers, men who wear dark clothing, printed kerchiefs, hats adorned with ribbons, and smiling black masks, represent African workers on the haciendas. Oral tradition tells that a young man was bitten by a snake while working in the countryside, and that his mother and the farmhands sang and stamped their feet around the animal to save his life. This story is staged with violin and guitar music and with plenty of footwork.

There are other versions. Some interpret it as a mockery of the landowners, which the workers carried out through the festival. Others see it as a memory of the pain and the resistance of the enslaved. And in some towns, the dance is performed to ask for good harvests or to heal. What is certain is that there is no single answer, and that the dance has taken on the meaning that each community gave it.

Look at the mask. The soft wood is carved, varnished in glossy black, and eyes, eyebrows, and a mustache are painted on. The smiling features make it friendly, almost mischievous: there is no anger in this face, only a smile that invites you closer. And the hat, covered with ribbons that hang down the back, gives it a festive air. It is a fine example of how folk art turns hard stories into spectacles of color.

Today there is debate about how to look at these masks. For some, they are a tribute to the African presence, and for others, an image that must be rethought with more care. In any case, they remind us of something important: that the history of Mexico includes many people who for a long time were absent from the books. A little while ago, in Oaxaca, you saw the [Diablos of the Costa Chica](mna_s17_mascara_diablos_costa), an Afro-descendant dance; here, another. They are two traces of the same thread.

With this mask our journey through the Gulf is nearly over, a region that began with the Olmec, in the halls downstairs, and reaches all the way to the music of violins. A great deal of time has passed between one and the other, but there is a common thread: the people who live here have always known how to turn what comes from the sea and the countryside into a culture of their own. One headdress remains, that of the Teenek women.

texto: Look for the mustache, the eyebrows, and the eyes of the mask
Observe the lined straw hat and the ribbons that fall down the back
Imagine the footwork that accompanies the dance

texto.Region: Totonacapan (Veracruz and the Northern Sierra of Puebla)
texto.Technique/Material: Carved cedar/coral tree wood, enamel, velvet, mirrors and satin
texto.Function: Ritual masking paraphernalia for the Dance of the Negritos (healing theater)

texto.pregunta: Myth: There was no African population in Mexico in colonial times.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Veracruz was the main port of entry for enslaved Africans into New Spain, and their legacy lives on in dances, music, and communities.
